protocol.instrument_name: NSW Pharmacist Practice Standards for Management of Gastro-Oesophageal Reflux and Gastro-Oesophageal Reflux Disease (Community Pharmacy Management of Gastro-oesophageal Reflux and Gastro-oesophageal Reflux Disease (GORD) Service)
protocol.instrument_version: NSW Health Authority dated 25 February 2026; approved 25 FEBRUARY 2026
protocol.legal_basis: NSW Health Authority (dated 25 February 2026); pharmacists must hold general registration under the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law and have successfully completed the training requirements detailed in the NSW Health Authority (dated 25 February 2026). Approved Medicines are listed in the NSW Health Authority (dated 25 February 2026).
protocol.supervision_model: approved pharmacist - appropriately trained approved pharmacists manage eligible patients as part of the NSW Health Authority (dated 25 February 2026); pharmacists must exercise professional discretion and judgement when applying the Practice Standard
protocol.scope_summary: NSW Health practice standard for approved pharmacists managing eligible patients (aged 18-50 inclusive) with gastro-oesophageal reflux or GORD in a community pharmacy: seven approved medicines (H2 receptor antagonists and proton pump inhibitors), assessment flowchart, consent, eligibility and red-flag referral criteria, 4-week supply limit, PPI stewardship and step-down therapy, 4-week review, documentation and communication requirements.

inclusion.text: Patients must be aged 18 years or over and up to and including aged 50 years to be eligible for the service.

provenance.section_heading: G. PATIENT ELIGIBILITY AND REFERRAL CRITERIA

inclusion.text: Patient presents to a participating approved pharmacist for management of gastro-oesophageal reflux or gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.
The patient has no red flags, or exclusions (checked against Section G).
Informed clinical and financial consent must be obtained from the patient prior to providing care under this practice standard.
Patients must be physically present in the pharmacy to be eligible for management.
Patients are required to have a consultation with an approved pharmacist before a medication can be supplied under the Authority.
To receive management for GORD under this service, the patient must fulfill the eligibility requirements of the Practice Standard.

exclusion.text: The patient has any 'red flag' warning sign (see box above).

steps.description: Patient presents to a participating approved pharmacist for management of gastro-oesophageal reflux or gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.
Is the patient >=18 years and <=50 years old? If No: 'Not eligible for management under the Authority and Practice Standard. Refer to GP.'

gates.criterion: Patient is >=18 years and <=50 years old

steps.description: Does the patient have any red flags, or exclusions? If Yes: 'Not eligible for management under the Authority and Practice Standard. Refer to Emergency Department or GP.'

gates.criterion: No red flags and no exclusions under Section G

steps.description: Conduct patient informed consent: Participation; Financial; Pharmacist communication with other health practitioners. If No: 'Not eligible for management under the Authority and Practice Standard. Refer to GP.'

gates.criterion: Informed consent obtained (participation, financial, communication with other health practitioners)

steps.description: Conduct patient history and clinical review including review of contraindications, precautions, drug interactions, pregnancy and lactation status.
Establish management plan.
Communicate agreed management plan with patient and patient's medical practitioner. Document all aspects of management plan.

Patient history should include: Age; Weight; Pregnancy and lactation status; Onset, nature, duration, frequency, severity, and pattern of symptoms; Precipitating and relieving factors; Underlying medical conditions and conditions that may complicate diagnosis; Dietary patterns; Current medication use (including prescribed medications, vitamins, herbs, supplements, over the counter medicines); Pharmacological and non-pharmacological (dietary and lifestyle) strategies trialled to treat symptoms and response; Drug allergies and adverse drug reactions; Smoking and vaping status; Alcohol and drug history. The My Health Record should be reviewed where appropriate and available.
Physical examination of patient as required. Assessment of vital signs.

'The Therapeutic Guidelines defines GORD as gastro-oesophageal reflux symptoms that are frequent (2 or more episodes per week) and severe enough to impair quality of life, or people who have complications of gastro-oesophageal reflux. However, the clinical definition of GORD may differ between resources used in clinical practice.' The cardinal symptoms of gastro-oesophageal reflux are heartburn and regurgitation. 'For adults who have typical symptoms and no red flag/alarm symptoms, response to a trial of PPI therapy can help to confirm the diagnosis of GORD.' 'A trial of high dose PPIs has a sensitivity of 80% as a diagnostic test for GORD.' Atypical symptoms attributed to reflux include belching, epigastric pain, dyspepsia and acid brash.

gates.criterion: Clear diagnosis of gastro-oesophageal reflux or GORD can be made from patient reported symptoms, history and PPI trial

steps.description: Assessment of chest pain and abdominal pain is complex, therefore maintain a high index of suspicion for differential conditions. Be aware of cognitive bias, focus on excluding red flags and early referral to a medical practitioner. 'Both GORD and acute myocardial infarction (AMI) can cause similar signs and symptoms, and frequently co-exist. Extreme caution must be exercised by pharmacists managing patients with suspected presentations of AMI. Pharmacists are required to immediately refer these patients to an emergency department for urgent medical assessment.'

gates.criterion: Acute myocardial infarction not suspected (no chest pain, signs or symptoms of myocardial infarction, or diaphoresis)

steps.description: Advise all patients with reflux symptoms to trial diet and lifestyle modification. Non-pharmacological/general measures: advice regarding dietary and lifestyle modification as per the Therapeutic Guidelines: Diet and lifestyle modification for the management of gastro-oesophageal reflux in adults.

The initial management of gastro-oesophageal reflux and GORD is based on the severity of symptoms and endoscopic findings (if known): classify as mild intermittent symptoms, or frequent or severe symptoms that significantly impair quality of life.
Mild intermittent symptoms require only diet and lifestyle modification or on-demand drug therapy.

Frequent or severe symptoms that significantly impair quality of life require regular therapy and may require further specialist intervention. These patients require a referral to a medical practitioner.

Pharmacotherapy as per the Therapeutic Guidelines: Management of mild intermittent symptoms of gastro-oesophageal reflux in adults; Management of frequent or severe symptoms of gastro-oesophageal disease (GORD) in adults; Gastro-oesophageal reflux during pregnancy. Approved Medicines: Famotidine, Nizatidine, Esomeprazole, Lansoprazole, Omeprazole, Pantoprazole, Rabeprazole; 'Ranitidine is permitted under this practice standard.' 'Pharmacists must only supply formulations listed in the Authority.' 'PPIs in pregnancy have different levels of evidence. Pharmacists must be guided by the most up to date evidence on the safety and efficacy of PPIs when providing management to pregnant and breastfeeding women.'

gates.criterion: Only formulations listed in the NSW Health Authority (dated 25 February 2026) are supplied
For pregnant and breastfeeding women, pharmacist is guided by the most up to date evidence on the safety and efficacy of PPIs

steps.description: 'The efficacy and availability of PPIs has led to PPI overuse. Long-term regular PPI therapy is only recommended for a limited number of indications and should be reviewed regularly. PPI therapy should be stopped if there is no ongoing indication.' 'Where regular drug therapy is required and a patient has not been previously reviewed by a medical practitioner, a referral to a medical practitioner is required.'

gates.criterion: Ongoing indication for long-term regular PPI therapy
Patient previously reviewed by a medical practitioner where regular drug therapy is required

steps.description: Assess response after 4 weeks of PPI therapy at the standard dose: is symptom control adequate?

gates.criterion: Adequate symptom control after 4 weeks of PPI therapy at the standard dose

steps.description: If initial PPI therapy provides adequate symptom control, therapy should be titrated down and continued at the lowest dose and frequency that controls symptoms, or eventually stopped - this is known as step-down therapy. Regular attempts should be made to further reduce the dose.

gates.criterion: Initial PPI therapy provides adequate symptom control

steps.description: 'If there is an inadequate response to treatment or symptom control is inadequate after 4 weeks of PPI therapy at the standard dose, the patient is required to be referred to a medical practitioner.'

gates.criterion: Inadequate response to treatment or inadequate symptom control after 4 weeks of PPI therapy at the standard dose

steps.description: Comprehensive advice and counselling (including supporting written information when required) as per the Therapeutic Guidelines, Australian Medicines Handbook, and other relevant references regarding: individual product and medicine use, including initial dosing, maintenance and step-down therapy; how to manage adverse effects; when to seek further care and/or treatment from a medical practitioner.

The agreed management plan must be documented in the patient electronic clinical record and shared with members of the patient's multidisciplinary team, in accordance with the Authority. Where a patient has a My Health Record, the pharmacist must ensure the details of the supply are uploaded to My Health Record, unless requested otherwise by the patient.

Clinical review with the pharmacist: if initial PPI therapy provides adequate symptom control, therapy should be titrated down and continued at the lowest dose and frequency that controls symptoms, or eventually stopped - this is known as step-down therapy. Regular attempts should be made to further reduce the dose.

gates.criterion: Initial PPI therapy provides adequate symptom control

steps.description: Where a patient requires long-term therapy for GORD, the patient must be referred to their medical practitioner for review and assessment.

gates.criterion: Patient requires long-term therapy for GORD

steps.description: Patients who have been appropriately reviewed and investigated for GORD by their medical practitioner and are presenting for repeat scripts can continue clinical reviews by the pharmacist.

gates.criterion: Patient appropriately reviewed and investigated for GORD by their medical practitioner and presenting for repeat scripts

steps.description: If the condition does not improve or resolve after 4 weeks of PPI therapy at the standard dose, the patient should be advised to see a medical practitioner for review and further investigation.

gates.criterion: Condition does not improve or resolve after 4 weeks of PPI therapy at the standard dose

red_flags.trigger_text: Extra-oesophageal symptoms that are associated with, but not specific to gastro-oesophageal reflux: tooth sensitivity, enamel erosion (particularly on palatal surface of upper incisors) and halitosis; pharyngeal and laryngeal signs and symptoms such as hoarseness and throat clearing, persistent cough, sore throat, pharyngitis and sinusitis; chest pain; sleep disturbance; nausea; asthma-like symptoms (cough, wheeze, shortness of breath) - 'These patients need to be referred to a medical practitioner for investigation and assessment.'

'Both GORD and acute myocardial infarction (AMI) can cause similar signs and symptoms, and frequently co-exist. Extreme caution must be exercised by pharmacists managing patients with suspected presentations of AMI. Pharmacists are required to immediately refer these patients to an emergency department for urgent medical assessment.'

'Some patients with features of GORD need to be referred to a medical practitioner for endoscopic investigation to rule out alternative aetiologies, confirm diagnosis of GORD and assess for complications (e.g. Barrett's oesophagus).'

Frequent or severe symptoms that significantly impair quality of life require regular therapy and may require further specialist intervention. These patients require a referral to a medical practitioner.
Where regular drug therapy is required and a patient has not been previously reviewed by a medical practitioner, a referral to a medical practitioner is required.
'If there is an inadequate response to treatment or symptom control is inadequate after 4 weeks of PPI therapy at the standard dose, the patient is required to be referred to a medical practitioner.'
'Where a patient requires long-term therapy for GORD, the patient must be referred to their medical practitioner for review and assessment.'

routine: Patients who have requested the service but are not eligible for management should be referred to their regular medical practitioner or health service.

Patients who meet any of the referral criteria below are not eligible for this service and must be referred to their regular medical practitioner or health service, or in instances of urgent care to the Emergency Department.
Pharmacists must apply clinical judgement and refer any patient considered appropriate for medical care for any reason.

Some patients with features of GORD need to be referred to a medical practitioner for endoscopic investigation to rule out alternative aetiologies, confirm diagnosis of GORD and assess for complications (e.g. Barrett's oesophagus).
Where regular drug therapy is required and a patient has not been previously reviewed by a medical practitioner, a referral to a medical practitioner is required.
Where a patient requires long-term therapy for GORD, the patient must be referred to their medical practitioner for review and assessment.
urgent: 'Red flag' warning signs that require immediate referral to a medical practitioner: Chest pain; Signs or symptoms of myocardial infarction; Any new symptoms or a change in symptoms in patients over the age of 50; Symptoms of anaemia including fatigue, shortness of breath, weakness, dizziness, or an irregular heartbeat; Difficult or painful swallowing; Haematemesis; Malaena; Vomiting; Jaundice; Unexplained weight loss; Severe, frequent, or changing symptoms; Abdominal pain; Diaphoresis
Red flag symptoms (also known as alarm symptoms, listed in the table above) are suggestive of other serious conditions and require immediate referral to a medical practitioner for assessment.
These patients require a referral to a medical practitioner (frequent or severe symptoms that significantly impair quality of life).
emergency: Pharmacists are required to immediately refer these patients to an emergency department for urgent medical assessment. (suspected presentations of acute myocardial infarction)
Not eligible for management under the Authority and Practice Standard. Refer to Emergency Department or GP. (flowchart, red flags/exclusions = Yes)

review_followup.when: At clinical review, if initial PPI therapy provides adequate symptom control
review_followup.what: Therapy should be titrated down and continued at the lowest dose and frequency that controls symptoms, or eventually stopped - step-down therapy. Regular attempts should be made to further reduce the dose.

review_followup.when: Where a patient requires long-term therapy for GORD
review_followup.what: The patient must be referred to their medical practitioner for review and assessment.

review_followup.when: Repeat script presentation (patient appropriately reviewed and investigated for GORD by their medical practitioner)
review_followup.what: Patients can continue clinical reviews by the pharmacist.

review_followup.when: After 4 weeks of PPI therapy at the standard dose without improvement or resolution
review_followup.what: The patient should be advised to see a medical practitioner for review and further investigation.
Long-term regular PPI therapy should be reviewed regularly and stopped if there is no ongoing indication.

review_followup.when: Within a week following the consultation (if the patient consents to disclosure)
review_followup.what: The record of the consultation and any subsequent consultations (including adverse events) must be shared with the patient's usual treating medical practitioner or medical practice, where the patient has one.

conditions: If the treating pharmacist becomes aware of an uncommon, unexpected or serious adverse event following treatment with an Approved Medicine, this should be reported to the Therapeutic Goods Administration. This should be conducted via the usual processes, by reporting online at https://aems.tga.gov.au/.
Additionally, you must notify the patient's usual medical practitioner (if they have one).
Where a patient has a My Health Record, the pharmacist must ensure the details of the supply are uploaded to My Health Record, unless requested otherwise by the patient.

open_questions.why_unclear: first_line set to false for all treatments; no agent is designated first-line in the document.

open_questions.topic: Red flag 'over the age of 50' overlaps with the eligibility upper age bound
open_questions.observed: 'Any new symptoms or a change in symptoms in patients over the age of 50' is a red flag, while eligibility is capped at 'up to and including aged 50 years' and exclusion EXC-3 removes patients aged over 50.
open_questions.why_unclear: The document does not explain how the red flag operates for patients who are already outside the age range; both statements recorded as printed.

open_questions.topic: Footnote markers on chest pain and abdominal pain only
open_questions.observed: 'Chest pain1' and 'Abdominal pain1' carry footnote marker 1 with the text 'Assessment of chest pain and abdominal pain is complex, therefore maintain a high index of suspicion for differential conditions. Be aware of cognitive bias, focus on excluding red flags and early referral to a medical practitioner.'
open_questions.why_unclear: Footnote transcribed into the trigger text for RF-1 and RF-12; no other red flag items carry footnotes.

open_questions.topic: Branch actions not stated for several gates
open_questions.observed: PW-3-S5 (pregnancy evidence gate), PW-3-S8, PW-3-S9, PW-4-S3 and PW-4-S4 use on_fail 'unclear'; the document does not state what happens when the pregnancy evidence check is not met, when adequate control is not achieved at step-down, when the repeat-script criteria are not met, or when the 4-week condition improves.
open_questions.why_unclear: Spec requires 'unclear' plus an open question where the document does not dictate the branch. PW-3-S2 severity branch and PW-1/PW-3 on_fail routing were inferred from adjacent prose (confidence medium on PW-3-S2).

open_questions.topic: GORD definition is hedged in the document
open_questions.observed: 'The Therapeutic Guidelines defines GORD as gastro-oesophageal reflux symptoms that are frequent (2 or more episodes per week) and severe enough to impair quality of life, or people who have complications of gastro-oesophageal reflux. However, the clinical definition of GORD may differ between resources used in clinical practice.'
open_questions.why_unclear: The document explicitly flags definitional variation; the 2-or-more-episodes-per-week threshold was captured in a pathway step with medium confidence rather than as a hard eligibility criterion.

open_questions.observed: referral.routine quotes from pages 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9; urgent from pages 5-6 and 8; emergency from pages 6 and 3.
open_questions.why_unclear: Spec requires one shared provenance object for the referral block using the first page; page range recorded here.

open_questions.observed: TGA reporting and notification of the patient's usual medical practitioner wording is on page 2; My Health Record upload requirement is on page 9 (repeated page 9 section K).
open_questions.why_unclear: Shared provenance uses the first page (2) per spec; range recorded here.

open_questions.topic: Referral criteria lists stated as not exhaustive
open_questions.observed: 'Note that these are not exhaustive lists.' and 'Pharmacists must apply clinical judgement and refer any patient considered appropriate for medical care for any reason.'
open_questions.why_unclear: The red-flag and exclusion lists cannot be treated as complete; the engine must allow pharmacist-initiated referral for any reason.
